card.hook: Four stone lions, a row of tall columns and a very grand flight of steps: the Fitzwilliam does not do shy. The good news is that it holds still, so it's the easiest posing partner in Cambridge.
card.stand_here: Cross Trumpington Street and stand on the far pavement opposite the main entrance. The museum is just to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot, so face it straight on with the portico in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural, front-on view. If the pavement is narrow and the whole building won't fit, tap 0.5x, or try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the columns, pediment and lions.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the centre of the portico on the middle line and keep the columns upright; if the sky looks too bright, tap the stonework and slide it a touch darker.
card.best_time: Soft daylight, like a bright overcast day or the morning, tends to suit the pale stone. Earlier in the day there are usually fewer people on the steps too.
card.selfie_here: Try beside Hobson's Conduit on Trumpington Street, where the museum's main entrance is in view. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if yours has it, and keep the entrance over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far pavement across Trumpington Street facing the portico, while you pose on the steps below the columns.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside is fine without flash, but skip selfie sticks indoors as they can get in other visitors' way. Check the museum's own photography policy and its site for restoration work before you go.
card.challenge: Get the portico dead centre with every column standing perfectly straight, and let the gridlines be your referee.
card.good_to_know: The museum was founded in 1816 under the will of Richard FitzWilliam, 7th Viscount FitzWilliam. The Founder's Building went up between 1837 and 1843 to designs by George Basevi, and C. R. Cockerell completed it. The carving, lions included, is by William Grinsell Nicholl, and the museum opened in 1848.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Cross Trumpington Street and stand on the far pavement opposite the main entrance. The museum is just to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot, so face it straight on with the portico in the middle of your screen.

card.hook: People have been trading on this patch since Saxon times, and the daily market still turns up with rows of coloured awnings. From above, it looks like a box of sweets dropped in the middle of old Cambridge.
card.stand_here: Stand at Great St Mary's: climb the tower and look down over the square. If you'd rather stay at street level, walk about 1 minute east into Market Hill itself and face the stalls, with the stone tower rising behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to take in the whole square from above, then try 0.5x for the full spread. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the awnings or King's College Chapel in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, line up the rows of stalls, and keep the chapel and rooftops in the upper third of the picture.
card.best_time: Go when the stalls are up, because the awnings are the whole point of the view from above. Check the official site for tower opening times before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Try the corner of Market Hill and Petty Cury, where the market square meets Petty Cury and the candy-coloured canopies are in view. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the canopies behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Take the right-hand passage alongside Great St Mary's into the square, then ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back and frame you with the church and the market stalls behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go up the tower. Keep a firm grip on your phone when you lean out over any edge.
card.challenge: Find the brightest awning in the square and get it in your shot with a college rooftop peeking out above it.
card.good_to_know: The square was mostly filled with buildings until a major fire in 1849 led to it being cleared. A Gothic Revival fountain went up in the middle in 1855 and most of it was pulled down in 1953. It once had a water supply from Hobson's Conduit, finished in 1614. The Guildhall on the south side was built in the 1930s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Great St Mary's: climb the tower and look down over the square. If you'd rather stay at street level, walk about 1 minute east into Market Hill itself and face the stalls, with the stone tower rising behind them.

card.hook: Here's a bridge that looks like one smooth curve but is secretly made of nothing except straight planks. Once you spot the criss-cross of timber, you can't unsee it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the public footpath of Silver Street Bridge, which is about a stone's throw southeast of the Mathematical Bridge. Face northwest toward the wooden arch, with Queens' College buildings behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic side view of the whole bridge with the college behind it. If people get in the way, tap 2x to pick out just the timber arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the bridge up along a horizontal line so the arch sits nice and level.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people. It can get busy with others taking the same picture, so be patient and take your turn at the rail.
card.selfie_here: Use the same spot on the Silver Street Bridge footpath, since it's the classic place to see the bridge. Turn your back to the wooden arch, switch to the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the bridge over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The Mathematical Bridge isn't a free public crossing, so enjoy it from the street. Respect any signs for private areas, and ask before you photograph people.
card.challenge: Take a few frames and wait for a punt to drift through, then pick the one where the boat sits just right under the arch.
card.good_to_know: William Etheridge designed the bridge and James Essex built it in 1749. It has been rebuilt twice, in 1866 and 1905, but keeps the same shape, and it's Grade II listed. You may hear that Isaac Newton built it without bolts, but he died over twenty years before it was built, so that one's a myth.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the public footpath of Silver Street Bridge, which is about a stone's throw southeast of the Mathematical Bridge. Face northwest toward the wooden arch, with Queens' College buildings behind it.

card.hook: On 28 February 1953, Francis Crick announced in this very pub that he and James Watson had 'discovered the secret of life'. Today it's a cream stone front on a narrow Cambridge street, and it's a lovely quick photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Bene't Street, directly opposite The Eagle. The pub front is to the north-west, across the street, so face it and put the central entrance in the middle of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit all three storeys. If you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x, but keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Use zoom 2x to get close to the blue plaque or the signage.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the entrance up with the middle vertical line so the street leads the eye to the door.
card.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the front. If the pale stone looks washed out, drag the brightness slider down a little after you tap the stonework.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the blue plaque next to the main entrance with the pub front behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit higher and keep it level. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more of the façade in the shot. If you're allowed into the courtyard, the galleried timber wing makes a lovely backdrop away from the street.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement east of the pub, facing west, while you stand in front of the pub so the whole front fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the front from the public street. The courtyard is inside the pub, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the blue plaque, the central door and one passing stranger all in the same frame, with the walls nice and straight.
card.good_to_know: The front dates from around 1600, and the pub opened in 1667 as a coaching inn. It's the second oldest pub in Cambridge. In the Second World War, Allied airmen wrote their names and squadron numbers on the ceiling of the rear bar.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Bene't Street, directly opposite The Eagle. The pub front is to the north-west, across the street, so face it and put the central entrance in the middle of your frame.

card.hook: Kettle's Yard looks like a row of ordinary old cottages, until you notice the plain modern bits stuck on beside them. That clash is your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in St Peter's churchyard, beside the church on Castle Street, and face across at the old cottage front of the house with the church close by in the frame. If the churchyard is closed, the Castle Street pavement works for a straight-on shot of the brick and glass front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the cottage front. Try 0.5x if you want more of the churchyard and church, and hold your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, then tap the brightest wall and nudge it a touch darker so the white window frames and sky don't glare.
card.best_time: A bright but softly cloudy day is ideal. Earlier or later in the day also works, with gentler light on the walls and a quieter street.
card.selfie_here: Try the gallery's entrance way on the west side of Castle Street, with the facade behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder. This one is a best guess, since no guide names it as a selfie spot.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a friendly passer-by in St Peter's churchyard and ask them to shoot across at the cottage front with you in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The churchyard view depends on it being open. Photography is allowed inside the House, but you have to check in your bags. Ask permission before photographing individuals or private property. The pavement from Pound Hill to the Castle Street entrance is quite narrow and steep in parts.
card.challenge: Play spot the difference: get the old cottage front and the plain new addition in one shot, with the walls perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: Kettle's Yard began as four small cottages that Jim and Helen Ede turned into one unusual home after moving to Cambridge in 1956. Jim gave the house and his early 20th-century art collection to the University of Cambridge in 1966. It reopened in February 2018 with new entrance and courtyard areas, so the frontage is newer than many older photos show.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in St Peter's churchyard, beside the church on Castle Street, and face across at the old cottage front of the house with the church close by in the frame. card.hook: A giant gold grasshopper is slowly munching on the seconds, and half the pavement is staring up at it. Welcome to the Corpus Clock, the one clock in Cambridge with no hands and no numbers.
card.stand_here: Cross to the opposite side of Trumpington Street, onto the corner across from the Corpus Clock, and face the Taylor Library wall at the corner of Bene't Street. Take care crossing, because the traffic never really stops.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from across the road so the whole clock and a bit of the corner fit in. Then try 2x for a tighter shot of the gold face and the grasshopper on top. Skip 0.5x for the clock itself, because it makes it look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gold face, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the blue lights stay crisp instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the blue lights glow and the traffic is lighter. Early morning is also worth a try if you want fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: The best bet is the pavement at the street-level corner where Trumpington Street meets Bene't Street, in front of the Taylor Library. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so you both fit, and keep the clock over your shoulder. It's busy and the traffic is constant, so keep well back from the kerb and be ready to take a few tries.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far pavement across Trumpington Street while you stand by the clock, so they can fit you and the whole clock in one shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Lots of people step into the road to get their photo, especially on the hour, but please don't. Stay on the pavement, because the traffic at this junction is constant.
card.challenge: Wait for the grasshopper to blink, then snap it mid-blink with its mouth going. Bonus points if your own reflection stays out of the shiny gold face.
card.good_to_know: The clock was unveiled in 2008 and sits in what used to be the entrance to a Victorian bank branch. The grasshopper-like creature on top is called the Chronophage, or 'time eater'. The face is gold-plated stainless steel, about 1.5 metres across, and blue lights shine through slits to show the hours, minutes and seconds.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Cross to the opposite side of Trumpington Street, onto the corner across from the Corpus Clock, and face the Taylor Library wall at the corner of Bene't Street. Take care crossing, because the traffic never really stops.

card.hook: Most people expect a famous library to look grand and fussy. The Wren Library looks calm and plain from the river, and that's exactly why it makes such a tidy photo: water, stone and sky, all lined up.
card.stand_here: Stand on Trinity Bridge. From there the library's river-facing side is to the north-east, with the Cam running in front of it, so face that way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole long building fits with the water in front. Tap 0.5x if you want more river and sky, or 2x to fill the frame with the row of windows and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the building up with a horizontal line, and keep a strip of river along the bottom.
card.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people on the bridge. Soft light from an overcast sky or the low sun shows off the stonework nicely.
card.selfie_here: Try the riverbank of the Cam outside the Wren Library, right beside the river-facing side. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x, and keep the library over your shoulder. Check the angle when you arrive, since you'll be working out how much of the building fits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Trinity Bridge while you stand on the riverbank, so they can get you with the library in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the library is not permitted, so make the outside your picture. Flash isn't allowed either, and the marble floors inside can be slippery, so watch your step. Check Trinity College's official site before you go, as opening hours are limited and the grounds can be restricted.
card.challenge: Get the library perfectly level on the gridline with a punt drifting through the river in front of it.
card.good_to_know: Christopher Wren designed the library in 1676 and it was completed in 1695. It's one big room built over an open colonnade in Nevile's Court, with large windows so readers had good light. Inside are rare books and manuscripts, including Isaac Newton's copy of the Principia and A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh manuscript.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Trinity Bridge. From there the library's river-facing side is to the north-east, with the Cam running in front of it, so face that way.

card.hook: Fourteen stone balls sit along Clare Bridge, and one of them has a chunk missing. Count them while you're up there, because it's the best excuse to slow down and look around.
card.stand_here: Stand on Clare Bridge, right in the middle. Turn to look back across the Cam at the college's river front, with the college just to the north-west of you.
card.zoom: Stay at zoom 1x to fit the river front, the bridge and King's College Chapel in one shot. Tap 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the roofline and the Chapel behind it. Zoom 0.5x only works if you want the stone balls huge in the foreground, and it can make the college look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the Chapel up so it sits behind the buildings instead of being cut off by a corner.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or in soft low light, when there are fewer people and the light is gentler. Evening is also worth a try from the Backs, where warm light hits the college's west-facing walls.
card.selfie_here: Stand mid-bridge on Clare Bridge with Old Court and the King's College Chapel view behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the view over your shoulder. The Fellows' and Scholars' Gardens along the river are another option, with the college buildings behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Garret Hostel Bridge facing downstream while you stay on Clare Bridge, since Old Court is visible from there.
card.rules_and_safety: Clare Bridge is inside college grounds, so follow the college's access rules and check the official site before you go. Access can be limited and the college is sometimes closed to visitors. The Fellows' Garden is open to the public mainly over the summer months after exams in June.
card.challenge: Spot the one stone ball with a piece missing, then get it in the corner of your photo as a frame.
card.good_to_know: Clare began in 1326 as University Hall and is the second-oldest surviving college in Cambridge, after Peterhouse. Clare Bridge dates from 1640 and is the oldest of Cambridge's current bridges. Old Court was built between 1638 and 1715 and is Grade I listed, and you can see the style shift from late Gothic to fully classical.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Clare Bridge, right in the middle. Turn to look back across the Cam at the college's river front, with the college just to the north-west of you.

card.hook: Water, lawn and a wall of Victorian glass, all in one frame, and you barely have to move to get it. Even the fountain plays along.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Main Lawn and face the glasshouses, with the fountain in front of you. Put the fountain low in the frame and let the glass rise neatly behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the fountain and glasshouses together. Go to 0.5x if the lawn is busy or you want more sky and planting, and try 2x to pick out the glasshouse roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the glass roofline level, then tap the glass or the fountain and make the picture a touch darker if the sky or glass looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft, in the morning or later in the afternoon. That's also when the lawn tends to be quieter. Check the official site for current opening times before you set off.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the bronze-leaf fountain on the edge of the Main Lawn with the glasshouse range behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the glass in, and hold the phone a little high. For a flowery alternative, the bee borders also have the glasshouses behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Main Lawn in front of the fountain and aim at you beside the fountain, so the Glasshouse Range shows behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos and selfies are fine, but drones aren't allowed anywhere in the garden. Portrait, wedding and commercial shoots need advance permission, and commercial photography isn't allowed inside the Glasshouse Range, so keep to outside views of the glass. It's a working garden with machinery in use, so keep clear of work areas while you pose.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the fountain and see which one catches the spray best, because moving water never looks the same twice.
card.good_to_know: Professor John Stevens Henslow, Charles Darwin's teacher, created the garden for the University in 1831, and it opened to the public in 1846. The lake was cleverly made from an old gravel pit, and the glasshouses date from the 1860s. Today the garden holds more than 8,000 plant species from around the world.

card.hook: Picture a small stone church with a pointy cone for a roof, squeezed in among taller buildings like it wandered in from the wrong century. That's the Round Church, and it's very hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Bridge Street and Round Church Street, on the Bridge Street side. Face the west front and the carved Norman doorway, and let the street edges frame the church for you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the church looks natural. If the pavement is too tight to fit the roof and doorway in, tap 0.5x. Go to 2x or higher to get close to the doorway carvings.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, hold your phone level so the walls stay upright, and put the doorway on one of the lines with the cone roof rising above it.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, before the sun drops behind St John's College. The church is low and the buildings around it are tall, so light only reaches it at certain times. The front can be in shadow in the morning, so tap the stonework and make it a bit brighter if it looks gloomy.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement at the corner where Round Church Street meets Bridge Street, with the church's west front behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your phone a little low so the cone roof and doorway fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on St John's Street, facing the church, and take your photo with the Round Church in view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Bridge Street is busy with delivery vans and cyclists, so wait for a gap before you shoot. Going early in the morning is quieter. This spot is about the outside view, as photography inside may not be welcome.
card.challenge: Can you get the doorway, the cone roof and your own grin in one shot without a single van sneaking in?
card.good_to_know: The church was built around 1130, and its round shape copies the rotunda of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. It began as a wayfarers' chapel beside the old Roman road that is now Bridge Street. It's one of only four medieval round churches still in use in England, and it has been Grade I listed since 1950.

card.hook: Imagine a pale Gothic chapel rising over a quiet river, with a cow chewing grass in the foreground. That's the Backs on a good morning, and yes, the cows are real.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Backs lawns beside Clare Bridge, at Clare College on the east bank of the River Cam. Face King's College Chapel, which is the classic view here.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the river, lawn and chapel all in one go. If the bridge is crowded, try 0.5x for more lawn and sky. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) brings the chapel closer without you moving.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the river along the lower third and the chapel on an upper line, then tap the pale stonework and slide it a little darker so the stone and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the punts and tour groups fill the river. You'll get the quietest version of this view.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on Clare Bridge itself, facing the river, with the Backs lawns and college buildings behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little low and wide, so the old bridge and the college look good over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on King's College Bridge and take your photo while you stand on the grass of the Backs, with King's College Chapel rising above the lawn behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The riverside paths are public, but some parts of the Backs are college grounds with limited access, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a grazing cow and make it your foreground, with the chapel standing tall behind it.
card.good_to_know: In 2013 National Trust chairman Simon Jenkins put the Backs in his top ten views in England. Since 1995 English Heritage has listed it as a Grade 1 Historic Park. It was once pasture, gardens and orchards, and Clare Bridge is described by guides as one of the oldest and best-known bridges here.

card.hook: King's Parade does half the work for you here. The Gothic front and tower of Great St Mary's sit right on the street, with King's College and its Chapel way off down the road. Your only job is to wait for the bikes to clear.
card.stand_here: Stand on King's Parade at the north end, opposite the Senate House, facing south down the street. Let the street lead your eye, with the church tower on one side of the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole street scene. If you're close and the tower won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x (or up to 5x on some phones) for a tighter shot of the tower and the carved stone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep your phone level so the tower doesn't lean. Then tap the stonework, and if the sky is bright, slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer on the street. Honestly, the view is worth a photo at any time of day.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit higher. Turn so the church tower is over your shoulder, and tilt up a touch to fit it all in.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on Senate House Hill, the short road at the north end of King's Parade, facing the church's front, while you pose in front of the church. A photo guide says the church should be in frame from there.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship and a university church, so be respectful if you go inside. Check the official site for visiting times and tower access. One visitor review says the tower roof was quite uneven, so take care up there. On the street, watch for cyclists and pedestrians before you step back to line up a shot.
card.challenge: Take one wide street shot, then walk closer and find the most interesting bit of carved stone for a second photo. Bonus points if no cyclist sneaks into the first one.
card.good_to_know: Great St Mary's is the University Church of Cambridge and a Grade I listed building. The church was built between 1478 and 1519, and the tower was finished later, in 1608. The University Clock inside chimes the Cambridge Quarters, which were later borrowed for Big Ben. Stephen Hawking's funeral was held here in 2018.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the Chapel, the Senate House and the street together. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Chapel's pinnacles at the far end.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up with a vertical grid line so the buildings stand straight, then let the street lead the eye to the Chapel.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, because the parade gets busy with visitors later in the day. If you're lucky enough to see snow, the Chapel has been photographed here in it.
card.selfie_here: Try Senate House Passage, the narrow passage by the Senate House, where you can look up toward King's Parade and the colleges. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the Caius and Trinity Hall buildings framing the view behind you. King's Parade itself won't be the main backdrop here, so check the framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement of King's Parade opposite the King's College gatehouse, facing it, while you stand toward the gate so the gatehouse and the Chapel behind it fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in public areas like King's Parade, but it's restricted inside King's College Chapel. Many college courts need permission for commercial shoots, so check with the porters' lodges.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap between cyclists, then try a Live Photo of one gliding through with the Chapel at the end, and pick your favourite frame afterwards.
card.good_to_know: The Senate House is mainly used for degree ceremonies, and this top end of the street is known as Senate House Hill. The college gatehouse and screen date from the 1830s, when the old west side of the street was cleared to make room for them. The Corpus Clock, added in 2008, sits at the southern end.

card.hook: Cambridge has a bridge that looks too pretty to be real, and you can't walk onto it unless you're inside St John's College. Lucky for you, the best free view is from the bridge next door.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kitchen Bridge, the Wren-designed bridge beside St John's College. Face across the River Cam toward the covered Bridge of Sighs, with the river filling the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the bridge, the river and a bit of the buildings around it. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the covered bridge. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of river and sky, and keep the bridge away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the Bridge of Sighs on one of the third lines with the river filling the lower part, then tap the pale stonework and slide darker if the sky is washing out the detail.
card.best_time: Pick a day with good weather, because that's when this view looks its best. Early or late in the day is likely to be quieter, and if it's busy, wait for people to move out of your shot.
card.selfie_here: Kitchen Bridge is the place for a selfie: use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze in more river and sky. The Bridge of Sighs is across the water in front of you, so it won't be over your shoulder here. For a picture of you with the bridge, use the passer-by shot below.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on the public riverside footpath at The Backs, looking across the Cam at the covered bridge between Third Court and New Court, to take your photo with the bridge in the view.
card.rules_and_safety: Kitchen Bridge is open to the public, but going into St John's College to walk the bridge or see its courts is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the arch sits neatly over its reflection, then spot a willow branch on The Backs and use it as a natural frame for a second one.
card.good_to_know: The Bridge of Sighs was designed by Henry Hutchinson in the Gothic Revival style and finished in 1831. It's Grade I listed. The name comes from the bridge in Venice, though the two have little in common beyond being covered and having arched bases. Queen Victoria is said to have loved it more than anywhere else in Cambridge, and it has appeared in The Theory of Everything and in a Pink Floyd video.

card.hook: In 1958, students got an Austin Seven van onto the roof of this building. Nobody's asking you to match that, but the roofline is still worth a good look.
card.stand_here: Stand on King's Parade, opposite the Senate House and near Great St Mary's. The Senate House is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot, so face that way and you'll see the whole front across the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the whole front in without bending it. If people or traffic push you closer, drop to 0.5x and keep the building in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) gets you the balcony, the roofline and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, then tap the pale stone and nudge it a touch darker so it doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Evening works well if you switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady. Otherwise, pick a moment when fewer people are walking through your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try Senate House Passage, the narrow lane between Gonville & Caius College and the Senate House, near the railings where the Senate House lawn shows through. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the building over your shoulder.

card.rules_and_safety: The Senate House isn't open to the public, so you'll be shooting from the street. The lawn may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the same front with different amounts of pavement and sky, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: James Gibbs designed the Senate House, and it was built in pale Portland stone between 1722 and 1730. The western end wasn't finished until 1768. It was meant to be one side of a quadrangle, but the rest never got built, so it stands alone. It's Grade I listed and mainly used for graduation ceremonies.

card.hook: Picture a punt drifting under a curved iron bridge while you stand at the water's edge with your phone out. That's Magdalene Bridge, and the river does half the work of making your photo look good.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Quayside, at the riverside edge of the quay on the Bridge Street side of the crossing. The bridge lies to the north-west of you, so face north-west and look back across the water at it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole bridge, the water and the punts. If you're standing too close for it all to fit, tap 0.5x. Try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the railings and the arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the arch near the middle with water filling the bottom third, then tap the bridge and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the ironwork keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to the water and the ironwork. Early in the day you'll usually have fewer punts in your way, though a punt in the shot adds nice scale.
card.selfie_here: We haven't found a proven spot for a selfie with the bridge behind you, so go general. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low and out so the bridge fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: If you want a shot of you with the whole bridge, ask a passer-by on the west bank of the River Cam to frame it for you (that's an old photo vantage rather than a marked spot, so check it works when you get there).
card.rules_and_safety: We haven't found any posted rules on selfie sticks here. The bridge is a public road and crossing and the Quayside is a riverside street, so keep an eye on traffic and other people. If you plan to visit any nearby colleges, check the official site first.

card.good_to_know: The iron bridge you see today dates from 1823 and was designed by Norwich architect Arthur Browne. It has been Grade II listed since 1969. Wooden bridges stood here from Anglo-Saxon times until James Essex built a stone one in 1754, and the original crossing is what gave Cambridge its name.

card.hook: Ask anyone to picture Cambridge and they'll probably see this chapel, but the best view isn't from the street. It's across the water meadow, with willows, the river and the long pale stone rising above the lawn.
card.stand_here: Stand in The Backs, on the far bank of the Cam, across the meadow from the Back Lawn. The chapel is to the east, so face east and you'll see its west end above the lawn and willows, with the river in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic view with the lawn, willows and river. Try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the west end and its pinnacles. Zoom 0.5x works for a low shot with willow branches or punts close in front, but the chapel will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the river or lawn in the bottom third, with the chapel's west end filling the space above it.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise if you can, when the footpaths are empty. Early is also the easiest time to find a good spot on the meadow.
card.selfie_here: Try the riverbank by Clare Bridge, where the chapel's west end comes into view across the lawn. Use the front camera, back up a little and turn so the chapel sits over your shoulder. It's worth checking the angle when you arrive. The lawn in King's College front court is another popular spot for a chapel selfie.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on The Backs, on the far bank of the Cam across the meadow from the chapel, so the whole building fits in the frame, while you stand a few steps in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: The chapel is still an active place of worship, so treat it as a working building. The college buildings are private, but you can photograph the grounds and the Back Lawn route to the river from outside. Check the official site before you go, as access can change.
card.challenge: Take one low zoom 0.5x shot with willow branches framing the chapel. Then zoom to 5x and see if you can pick out the pinnacles on the west end.
card.good_to_know: King's College Chapel was built in phases by a succession of English kings between the mid-1400s and 1515. It holds the world's largest fan vault, finished in 1515 by master mason John Wastell. It's also the home of the King's College Choir.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in The Backs, on the far bank of the Cam, across the meadow from the Back Lawn. The chapel is to the east, so face east and you'll see its west end above the lawn and willows, with the river in front of you.

card.hook: Henry VIII has been glaring down at Trinity Street since the college began, and he's the star of this shot. Your only rival is a delivery van that thinks the cobbles are its own.
card.stand_here: Stand on the cobbles on Trinity Street, right in front of the Great Gate. Face the gate, with the college lying behind it to the west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole Great Gate frontage in. If the street is too tight, tap 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out Henry VIII above the archway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the gate up square-on so the stonework stays straight, then tap the stonework and drag the slider to make it a little darker if the sky is washing out the top.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the sun lights the frontage and the crowds haven't arrived. If a van is blocking the cobbles, shift a few steps and wait for a clear moment.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the cobbles in front of the Great Gate, switch to your front camera and keep the gate over your shoulder. For a different backdrop, try the steep Garret Hostel Bridge over the Cam (reached via Garret Hostel Lane), with Trinity College in the view behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the cobbles in front of the Great Gate and ask a passer-by to frame you with the whole gate behind you, ideally in the morning when it's fully lit.
card.rules_and_safety: The college grounds are private and visitors must not walk on the grass lawns. Photos for commercial purposes need written permission from the Junior Bursar in advance.
card.challenge: Take a shot where the gate's stone edges are dead straight and Henry VIII looks like he's keeping an eye on you.
card.good_to_know: Henry VIII founded Trinity in 1546 by merging two older colleges, Michaelhouse and King's Hall. Behind the gate is Great Court, said to be the largest enclosed courtyard in Europe. Most of the major buildings date from the 16th and 17th centuries.

card.hook: A punt drifts under a stone bridge, a willow dips toward the water, and you've got about ten seconds to get the shot. That's the Bridge of Sighs from upstream, and it's very good at making a phone photo look planned.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kitchen Bridge, upstream of the Bridge of Sighs. Face back toward the college, so the Bridge of Sighs arches over the Cam beside the New Court buildings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits stonework, water and boats in one shot. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the bridge's stonework. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want lots of sky and water, and keep the bridge away from the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the brightness down to darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early. It's usually quieter on the bridge and the river, and the gentler light suits the stonework. Bright midday sun can make the buildings and water look flat or glary.
card.selfie_here: Kitchen Bridge is the best-documented spot for a photo with the Bridge of Sighs in view. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and turn until the bridge shows over your shoulder. Check the screen, because the exact angle isn't confirmed.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on The Backs footpath, where the Bridge of Sighs is clearly visible, to take your photo: you stand on the path with the bridge behind you and they step back to fit it all in.
card.rules_and_safety: Kitchen Bridge is on college land, and photography on College property is restricted and often needs prior permission. Check the St John's College website before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the bridge on a third-line, and wait for a punt to float into the bottom of the frame. Bonus points if nobody in the punt is waving.
card.good_to_know: St John's was founded by Lady Margaret Beaufort, and its charter is dated 9 April 1511. The site beside the Cam was once a medieval hospital, and today the college has eleven courts. Its chapel, designed by George Gilbert Scott, is the third tallest building in Cambridge.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Kitchen Bridge, upstream of the Bridge of Sighs. Face back toward the college, so the Bridge of Sighs arches over the Cam beside the New Court buildings.

card.hook: Everyone comes for the wooden arch, and then a punt glides underneath and suddenly your photo has a little story in it. Queens' College is a very good place to be patient.
card.stand_here: Stand on Silver Street Bridge, which is about a hundred feet from the Mathematical Bridge. Face upstream across the River Cam so the wooden arch fills the view, with the old brick courts rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole arch and the brick buildings. If the bridge railing or other people crowd you, drop to 0.5x. Or try 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the bridge and the courts without moving.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the arch along the lower third so the brick courts get room above it, then tap the wooden bridge and drag a bit darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Earlier in the day is often calmer on the bridge, and the softer daylight is kind to brickwork. Any time works if you're patient enough to wait for a punt.
card.selfie_here: If you go into the college, try the Cloister Court arches. Stand under them facing into the courtyard, use the front camera, and let the repeating arches fill in behind you. Check the official site first to see whether you can go in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Silver Street Bridge, looking upstream at the wooden bridge, to take your photo with the arch behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Mathematical Bridge is reserved for college members, so photograph it from outside rather than walking across. The college itself may charge for entry, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a punt right under the arch, then take one in portrait and one in landscape and see which one wins.
card.good_to_know: Queens' College was founded in 1448 by Margaret of Anjou and refounded in 1465 by Elizabeth Woodville, which is why the apostrophe comes after the s. It's one of only two Cambridge colleges whose main buildings straddle the River Cam, with the two halves joined by the Mathematical Bridge. The Old Court is described as one of the best-preserved medieval groups of buildings in the city.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Silver Street Bridge, which is about a hundred feet from the Mathematical Bridge. Face upstream across the River Cam so the wooden arch fills the view, with the old brick courts rising behind it.
